speechtext:
Can the minister give
us any information with regard to the question of establishing an ore dressing plant in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
When I
came to the department there was a vote in the estimates for the construction of a plant, but we did not go on with the construction; instead we put in a vote for a year or two for the transporting of the ores down here and their testing in the laboratory. However, there was very little advantage taken of that
Supply-M ines

provision, and I have cut the vote this year, but we are prepared to make all these tests and carry the ore down free of charge to the prospector.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
I think perhaps the main
reason why this has not been taken advantage of is that the distance is great, and the quantity that can be sent is small, and other than in some odd specific cases it would scarcely be applicable. The minister is aware of, and I know he is quite sympathetic with the immense development in mining in British Columbia; the same applies also to northern Ontario and northern Quebec, but I am speaking now of British Columbia particularly, and of the existence there of a great-variety of minerals, some of which are minerals of commercial value, and others of a more complex nature. What struck me when I was over in the Old Country last autumn and saw the display of minerals in the Canadian building at Wembley-not at the government's expense, I want to make that clear-* was this, and I mentioned it to some of the officials in charge. I think'it would have been very desirable if we could have shown in greater exactness and more detail the availability of these minerals, the quantities, and so forth; because I discussed with some industrialists over there certain matters regarding minerals in Canada, and they seemed not to be very well informed.
An ore dressing plant such as has been suggested, if established in British Columbia to deal with some of our complex ores, might be able to find a system of handling them that would enable us to get into the world market minerals that are at present in the country, but are not being recovered at commercial values at the present time. Of course, it would be of tremendous advantage to the country at large if some of these mineral resources could be so developed. I know the difficulty about the establishment of such a plant. There is the question of locality; personally, I am not mentioning locality at all. All I want to see is an ore dresing plant situated where it can be utilized, and that is a question for the minister's officials to deal with.
In addition to that, there is the question of just how to get the plant operating so as to get the most benefit from it. This vote of $5,000 by which ores can be sent in small packages three and in some cases over four thousand miles, coming from northern British Columbia, is not, I submit, of very much value. I am not criticizing the existence of the vote, but I do not think it meets the case. I would suggest to the minister that

this whole question should be taken up again, having in mind a genuine endeavour to market in a commercial way the various metals and minerals that we have in Canada. I have expressed myself imperfectly, but I think the minister will grasp what I mean. I think that the establishment of an ore dressing plant, or some other method, if there is a better one, of ascertaining the values of these ores and working out a commercial process for marketing the minerals would! justify some effort and some expenditure.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
I am in thorough
accord with the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I am quite convinced, and have been for some time, that it is necessary to have some method of treating and dressing the ores of the different provinces, and especially those found in the province of British Columbia. We have an abundance of complex ores in that province, and it is only necessary for them to be treated to_ a certain extent. If advantage has not been taken of the provision whereby ores can be transported free to the testing station here at Ottawa, I think it is because of the distance, and also because the results of these tests do not go (far enough. I have had representations made to me that while the results obtained from the department arw very good in respect to defining the content of these ores, the department might go further and furnish the values of the minerals that are to be found in these ores. The principal part of this work is really done by the prospector. He goes out into the mountains and discovers certain deposits. He sends samples to the department here to find out what they contain. When he gets the findings, he must go still further and send the result of these tests to the assayer to ascertain the values. I believe it would be of great assistance to the prospector, who is the pioneer in the mining industry, if the department would also furnish the values with the result of their tests. It has also been brought to my attention that the private institutions connected with the mining industry of British Columbia do at the present time furnish these tests. They carry on a certain amount of that work, and they also give the values in connection with their tests. But with the increased activity in mining, these private institutions will be unable to go that far on account of the many requests that are coming to them, and it has been represented to me that inquiry be made of the government as to whether the department here could not furnish the values. I am well aware that

Supply-Mines
such a privilege could be abused to some extent by large corporations, if they saw fit to take advantage of it, but I believe that the request in this matter has been asked on behalf of the pioneer prospector, and such a provision would be of great assistance to him.

speechtext:
The question asked by my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Simpson) brought up a subject on which I wish to make a few remarks^ and I think they will be as applicable here as on any other item. I refer to the iron ore bounty. My hon. friend coming from that section, like myself, is naturally interested-and so, I believe, is the whole country-in this question. While the minister said that they had not yet decided to recommend any co-operation with the provincial government, at the same time I should like to impress upon him, as the hon. member for West Algoma and others have done on previous occasions, the importance of giving very serious consideration to the question. It is not just a local question. One of the reasons why the National Railways, indeed all the railways in this country, have found it difficult to carry on has been a shortage of freight, and that is particularly due to the lack of population in that gap of more or less unsettled country between North Bay and the Manitoba boundary. We have an area there as large as the British Isles and the German Empire combined, and yet while they have one hundred and ten millions of people, or thereabouts, in those European countries we only have in this northern Ontario section about 150,000, so that this area forms an immense gap where neither passenger nor * freight traffic, nor population, is as large as it should be. Therefore the whole of Canada, -as well as northern Ontario, is interested in developing the iron industry which is one of the basic industries in commercial processes throughout the world. There is no country in the world that is really a great commercial country that has not its prosperous iron industry; and there is this further fact to be remembered in our case that we import from the United States something like $150,000,000 or $175,000,000 worth of iron and iron products each year. I should think that, in view of the past history of this country in helping various industries with bounties, enterprises which have been built up into very large industries, the government might well, consider co-operating with the province of Ontario which has proposed to grant a bounty in unison with another bounty from the Dominion government. I think the government might very well give
very serious consideration to that idea between now and the next session of parliament. I do not believe that at this late day in the session there would be any likelihood of bringing the proposition to a successful issue; but this is a question which has been a very live one, which is being agitated very strongly not only in northern Ontario, and down in the Maritime provinces, but in British Columbia as well. We have also heard of deposits being found in Manitoba; that province has ore deposits which also might be utilized in the same way. There is this fact to be remembered too: If we offered a bounty, in co-operation with the bounty proposed by the government of Ontario, and the project were not a success there would be no money spent. There is a further fact to be borne in mind. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has pointed out on the floor of the House on different occasions-I heard him do it some years ago-the great success that was met in the case of the steel industry in Canada through the bounties that were given by the Liberal government between 1896 and 1906, or thereabouts. I believe that even my hon. friends to the left who are free traders-or a large number of them,-if they were convinced that a bounty for a time would start a basic industry such as this, would probably not feel that it was as harmful a type of protection as they consider some of the other forms are.

But even if there were, I have read a statement on the question of -protection by many of the best authorities, professors of political economy and others, to the effect that the bounty system is the least vicious-using my hon. friend's term-because it is a straightforward method, you know exactly what you give and what returns you get, and in many cases there is no possibility of building up the desired industry -by any other means. However, that is by the way. I just wish to impress upon the minister once again the necessity of a serious consideration of the whole question; and I hope that between this
Supply-M ines

and next year the government may give some thought to this question-as has been given in the past by various governments-the granting of iron ore bounties on the line of the steel bounty, the lead and 4 p.m. zinc bounty, the oil bounty, and various others. speechtext: Is the government considering any scheme for the development of the iron and steel industry-that is the utilization of our great deposits of iron ore- in a manner similar to that adopted by the British government under the Aids to Industry Act? Has there been any proposal for, or consideration of, a plan of that kind, in contra-distinction to the bounty system, or supplementary thereto?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
May I say in reply to my hon. friend first, that I am not familiar with the details, but I believe a proposal of that kind has been discussed between members of the government and representatives from British Columbia, but I do not think any action has been taken on the matter at the moment, although a considerable amount of discussion has occurred. But, dealing with the question raised by the hon. member for Fort William and: Rainy River, namely, the question of assisting in the development of the iron industry in Canada

by way of a bounty, let me say that I do not go the length to which my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) goes in characterizing this as a most vicious kind of protection. So far as the Mines branch of the federal government is concerned at the present moment, having in mind perhaps that the most important service that could be rendered would be the evolving of a process of dealing with these low grade ores, that we are bending all our energies, working in conjunction with the American Department of Mines or any other informative source that we can find, to ascertaining whether or not a process can be developed that will make it profitable to mine and transform into pig iron the low grade iron ore that we have in Canada in large quantities. There is no question but that if that could be done we would be in a very different position in Canada from the one we now occupy; and that many of the things suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) would come about. We are very much alive to the importance of the question, and feel that perhaps we can render a great service at tlje moment by investigating every one of these processes that comes under our notice. At the moment we are working on an electrical process that we hope will prove a partial solution at least. I hope that before long some one will evolve a commercially feasible process. I can quite appreciate the desire of the Ontario government to lend encouragement along the same line; but we feel that for the time being we can best serve the development of this industry by what we are doing to-day.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES

speechtext:
I am not just dear
on this question of testing or treating ores. Would the minister explain the procedure in regard to testing a shipment of ore coming to headquarters at Ottawa? Have the department had any requests in regard to furnishing assays of ores that are sent in?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
We are not
attempting to do this work in any commercial way. I think the hon. member mentioned the fact that the prospector was not in a position to get tests made for iwhich he would have . to pay. That is just the field that we are trying to fill, to test all the discoveries of the prospector. I do not say that we are confining our efforts entirely to that, but our chief desire is to lend that aid to the individual who has spent his time and money in trying to discover mineral. After the assay is made and the various minerals that usually are found in the sample are discovered, we try to work out a process that we can give him for his information. We advise him as to what the ore contains in pounds and as to the ibe^t method of treating and handling that particular sample. It is true that we do not furnish the actual dollars-and-cents value of the product, but that can easily be ascertained when he has at his disposal those two or three very important pieces of information.
In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), we put no restrictions on the quantity which may be sent forward for investigational work here. I do not think the government of Canada should be called upon to provide a commercial plant. We are
Supply-Mines

doing our full duty by carrying out investigational work rather than by attempting to enter the commercial field or to develop this work in a large way, employing a number of highly technical men and machinery for the purpose of testing ores in big quantities.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
That was the point
I was interested in. I am not concerned in any way with the commercial end of the matter; I am interested in providing some way of assisting the prospector, the one who goes out and actually finds the mineral. I can go as far as to say that I have not had any representations made to me on behalf of the commercial phase of the question. When the prospector sends 'his ore to the testing plant at Ottawa, at the time this test is made, it might be very easy to assist him by providing an assay giving the value in dollars and cents of the metal content. If he sends his ore to the plant here and a report as to the result of the test is furnished to him, he then has to send the result of that test to an assayer. That takes a good deal of time and money, and prospectors are not in a position to do that. The fees in connection with assaying are fairly high, and if the man is constantly engaged in prospecting, he has to have a good many assays made in a season. Therefore, when the department has the prospector's ores here, it might go as far as to give him the value of the metal content in dollars and cents and he would then have the result of his season's investigation right before him. I do not think, for a moment, anyone wishes the department to look at this matter from the commercial angle. All the big commercial institutions engaged in mining carry on extensive assaying and testing plants of their own, and' it is hardly necessary for commercial institutions to call upon the department.

speechtext: Has any investigation ever been made as to the metals in the Rocky mountains? We are under the cloud) of a great national debt which, if it is to be paid, must be paid through the development of our natural resources. speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
We are
doing geological work in the mountains every year; whenever reports are 'brought to us we try to investigate the possibilities of new discoveries.

speechtext: With regard to the question of peat, I remember that a few years ago, in an effort to get rich quick, I lost in peat all the money I had. I had not followed the developments in the last five or six years but I understood the minister to say that progress had been made. I should like to know something about the cost of manufacture, what the finished product can be sold* for, and whether any is now being sold commercially.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext: The experiments were carried out at Alfred, between here and Montreal, and we did not discover that there was any short process for drying the peat. They simply spread the mud, as I call it, on the ground and left it to be dried by the sun.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES

The rain
does not affect it except that it takes longer to dry.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext: When it is wet it disintegrates and the whole process has to be gone over again. We found that we could never get enough dried.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
So far as
I could ascertain down here, and I watched it closely, the whole thing depended upon the devolpment of machinery to handle the material cheaply. I have given an opportunity to everyone who has come along with a pressure process, or with some process of sun-drying, to try it out. There is an engineer here who felt that he was discriminated against because we had not given him the necessary machinery to put his process to the test, and we decided to meet his wishes in this regard. So far no process has been discovered whereby you can separate the moisture content from the peat, the composition being about 90 per cent moisture and 10 per cent solid matter. It seems impossible to bring sufficient pressure to bear to extract all the

moisture to make it decent fuel. We had an area covered with the peat and we produced about 4,000 tons in a short time.

how much work the Mines department was doing in actual investigation. The minister was not able to give me an answer to that question.

speechtext: There is a doubt in my mind as to whether we are spending this money effectively in developing our already known deposits. I spent two or three days in that district, and I do not think I ever heard so many complaints in so short a time from prospectors and others interested in mining. It seems to me the whole thing has been done in a haphazard way as far as that important mineralized section is concerned.

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES

my hon. friend's first visit to a mining field?

it likely.

when hard-working men-and these prospectors are hard-working men-complain that they are being neglected.

This district in The Pas is one hundred miles from the nearest town. In coming out from there I was accompanied

by prospectors who were on their way to register their claims a hundred miles from the mining district. It seems to me that is an undue hardship imposed on men who are all the time undergoing great hardships in trying to investigate our mineral deposits. I think the real work of investigating our mineral deposits is being done by the prospectors, and I do not think much assistance is given by the department. I know that a great many of their hardships were not really due to the neglect of the department, but I say that if this department were supervising the districts where there .'are 'probably a thousand men or more on their own responsibility engaged in a work of national importance. and if the department were directing their minds towards that district in any systematic way, a lot of things such as railway facilities, for instance, and post office facilities, might be provided-[DOT]

subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES

My hon.
friend is not blaming the mining proposition for the lack of railways and post offices?

speechtext: These things are due to the lack of consideration. by this department. friend asked me the cost.

	,
to grant me a test upon this sample, and the way in which he put it was this: "How are we to know that this is a genuine sample?" I could only give him my word ol honour. area such as The Pas mineral belt this government. should have some official with some knowledge of the situation, helping the prospectors, and giving them advice, and trying to lessen the amount of hazard there is in their work. you guide, a prospector?

not making light, or attempting to make light, of it. I think a great deal of the prospectors, and they have done a great deal for Canada; but you go beyond1 the point when you say anyone can guide a prospector when he is out looking for minerals.

there are many ways a prospector can be helped, especially as to the quality of his find.

We are
doing that. We are taking the samples from the prospector at the nearest station, paying the freight on these samples to Ottawa, and when they are examined we issue a statement with respect to them, and that statement is

But I hope my hon. friend does not think there is any way of our organizing a search for minerals. That has always been done by the prospectors, in whom he is interested, and in whom I also, am interested. The prospector is the man I want to help because he is the real pioneer in mineral development; he has to put up with all the difficulties he meets with in going into the unbroken wilds. If he thinks he has found anything we can give him expert advice on it. It is true he has to go a long distance to register his claim, but we could not establish recording offices in every centre. We are not
doing anything with peat at the moment except endeavouring to discover whether there is any better process, because we consider that so far as the air drying process is concerned we have solved that problem. The peat bogs of Canada are not nearly so old as those of Ireland, and you cannot treat them in the same way. There is a tremendous amount of water in our peat, and we think we have solved the drying problem by the air drying process, so that peat can now be marketed within a reasonable distance of the bog itself in a commercial way, and become a reasonable adjunct to the other fuels, but we are still willing to investigate, although we are not spending any large amount of money, any process of pressure that might be discovered that would seem to shorten up the drying process.

Mr. HUMPHREY; I wish to come back to the question of mineral ores, in which there is a little more money than in peat. With reference to the remarks made by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) I may say that so far as I am personally concerned I have lived a lifetime with the prospector and there is no one who has a greater respect or a higher regard for the prospector than I have. The prospector is not a man who will be guided when it comes to prospecting in the hills. The kind of assistance a prospector wants is a grub stake, and it is not through some organization that the prospector functions. But he does want assistance from the different governments, I quite admit that; and I am afraid that the assistance that is being given to the prospector is falling off to some extent. While no headquarters organization will ever be able to guide the prospector in any shape or form, he does need assistance in determining the content and the values of his discoveries. With regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Nelson in reference to the work of the Mines department, I must disagree with him. From my own personal experience and the experience of others, I know that the Mines department has been doing a wonderful work in developing the mining industry in British Columbia. I cannot speak for Manitoba, but I can say that the wonderful activity in mining that is taking place in British Columbia at the present time is due to the research and scientific methods that have been discovered and approved by the Department of Mines. I would like the federal government to go further and give every possible assistance to the prospector by telling him what is in his ore and the values. That is the one point I would like to urge upon the minister.
As far as the geological work and other work that has been done by the Mines department in the past is concerned, I can only commend it. As a result of that work, mining engineers are now able to go into different localities in the several provinces without any waste of time or money and develop the mineral resources there. In that way the Mines department, while I will not say it has done everything possible, has assisted the mining industry to a very great extent, and
Supply-M ines

I only hope that they will continue to work along these lines, because the actual results that have been brought to my notice speak very highly of the work of the department. There is, however, need of a good deal of co-operation between the provincial governments. Of course, we fully understand that the mineral resources in the province of Manitoba are in a somewhat different position from those in British Columbia, because in Manitoba they are under the control of the Dominion government, whereas in British Columbia, outside of the Dominion belt, they are under the control of the province, and it is through road building and in other ways that help is given to the prospector. In the past few years I know that the number of prospectors throughout the Dominion has been falling off. I trust this is not due to lack of assistance from our federal and provincial governments.
Mr. LeSUEUR:	During the sessions of
1923 and 1924 the status of the oil fields and the oil industry in Lambton and Kent counties was argued at some length in this House, and after much urging the government consented to an investigation. My information is that Dr. G. S. Hume, the geological expert, and Mr. Russell, an expert more I presume in financial matters, went up there and made an investigation at considerable length, with the assistance they could receive in that section. The situation of the oil fields and of the oil industry in those two counties, Lambton and Kent, is so serious, and was so serious, that those interested sent for the third time in the third successive session a deputation to Ottawa to take up with the government the question of continuing the assistance which has been given to them by way of bounty. To my mind it was most important that the reports of these two gentlemen should be before the House and before the government in considering the request of that deputation, and for that purpose I put a motion on the order paper asking for a copy of the instructions given to Dr. Hume and Mr. Russell in connection with their visit to the county of Lambton, and of all letters or reports written or made by them or either of them thereon, and all correspondence relating thereto. The return, to that order I have here, No. 187, and it reads in part as follows:
A copy of the instructions issued to Dr. Hume covered by this order is attached hereto.
Passing on, the meat of the return is this:
No report on the Kent and Lambton counties fields was requested from Dr. Hume in the instructions issued to him, and none was made, nor will any be made by 
him thereunder. There is no information on file in the Department of Mines concerning instructions to, or a report by Mr. Russell.
I have brought this matter up because I thought these reports were most important in the event of either the government or this House deciding on the question of continuing the bounty in the Kent and Lambton oil fields. To the producers in those fields this is really a matter of life and death, as was explained in the arguments on this subject formerly presented in this House. My information was that Dr. Hume did make a full report to the department, and that Mr. Russell also made an exhaustive investigation and reported to the government. When I received the return saying there was no report and no report expected, I took it up with a gentleman who had been to Ottawa in three successive years with these deputations to the government, and 1 wish to read what he writes in reply:-
Your letter of April 25, last, advising of the result of your effort to get before the House Dr. Hume's report on the condition of our oil industry here was received in due course.
While it may be true that no report was requested from Dr. Hume when he received his instructions to visit and investigate this field it is hard to understand a government official, at the country's expense, going to the trouble of making such an investigation and not being required to report back the result of such investigation.
Very soon after his arrival here Dr. Hume saw me and explained to me the purpose of his visit. I raised the question of the effect of the removal of bounty on oil and he then told me that he was not here under any instructions from the government to secure information in connection with the bounty controversy but that the object of his visit was to secure some information for his own particular department. He then stated that he thought it quite proper and necessary to report to his department his opinion of the result of the removal of the bounty and he asked that we give him such information as we had on the bounty subject.
Every facility was given Dr. Hume to make a thorough investigation and following his investigation a meeting of our producers was held attended by Dr. Hume and at this meeting the bounty matter was fully gone into and Dr. Hume made rather copious notes as to what was said. Following this meeting of our producers Dr. Hume prepared a report for his department at Ottawa and as he wras not returning to Ottawa from here it was his intention to forward this report by mail. Before posting it Dr. Hume called upon me at my office, read the report to me, made some changes suggested by me and stated that it would be forward to Dr. Camsell that day, Friday of the week. I was in Ottawa on the Monday following the Friday Dr. Hume was in my office, saw Dr. Camsell in his office on Monday morning, he admitted to me that he had just received Dr. Hume's report, that he had not had an opportunity to read and consider it but that he purposed having some copies made and would go into the matter later on. As a result of some of my efforts the Minister of Mines, Hon. Mr. Stewart had Dr. Camsell call at his, Mr. Stewart's office, with the report and I saw two typewritten copies of the report in Dr. Camsell's possession in Mr. Stewart's office.

Supply-M ines
I have gone into this matter with considerable detail because I believe that when all these particulars are brought to the government's knowledge they will realize that a blunder has been made some place when the return was brought down declaring that Dr. Hume had never made any report. I believe we are entitled to have this oil bounty matter discussed upon its merits and are entitled to have this report as well as the material and information collected by Mr. Russell submitted to the House.
Yours truly,
I. Greenizen.
I believe that an injustice 'has been done to these fields lor the numerous reasons which have been thoroughly threshed out already. This investigation, in my opinion, has thoroughly corroborated every statement made in the House in regard to the situation in these two oil fields. It was therefore with the utmost surprise that I read the statement in the return that no such reports had been made. I wrote to Petrolea about the matter, and the reply is what I have read.

Dr. Hume's instructions were to visit that field on his way west and to make an investigation for the information of the deputy minister-for his information alone and for the benefit of no one else-as to the situation with respect to oil alone and not with respect to bounties. The granting of a bounty, or otherwise, is a matter of policy. Mr. Fielding, rightly or wrongly reduced the bounties and since that time a gentleman-I have forgotten his name, but he has been here on several occasions- has been in my office repeatedly. He has pointed out that the production has fallen to such a low point that ruin would absolutely ensue unless the bounties were continued. Let me say frankly that speaking personally I never concealed the belief that in the event of oil being discovered in large quantities in Canada the amount of bounty paid would ruin the country, but so long as the bounty was confined to the Ontario fields it would not be a serious matter. I take full responsibility for advising these producers that I thought the industry was surely now in the position to carry on without assistance from the federal government. I 5 p.m. merely mention that in passing.
Coming back to Dr. Hume, his report was of a confidential character; I cannot speak for Mr. Russell, I do not know why Mr. Russell was sent there, and I have no knowledge that he did make a report. If Mr. Russell was sent there officially to prepare a report, I have no complaint to make, but the point is this:	Where a question of
policy is concerned I do not think it is the business of a government official to pass his opinion upon it. He is an expert in his own
line, but cannot be accepted as an authority on matters of policy-as to what ought to be done in the way of reducing or enlarging bounties, or otherwise.
Mr. LeSUEUR: The first point made by the minister as to the ruining of the country by leaving this bounty on in the event of a large production is easily answered by the suggestion made by the deputation that the bounty should only be applicable to the first five barrels per well, or to some limited amount per well, which would answer fully the purpose and avoid entirely the possibility that the minister mentioned1. But now, the point is this:	The reply given in the return says
that no report on the Kent and Lambton fields was requested from Dr. Hume in the instructions issued to him, "and none was made nor will any be made by him thereunder." Now, the minister admits there was a report. Whe.her that report was confidential or not, it was a report; yet a return was brought down to the House which contained a statement to the contrary, and which, according to the minister's own statement is not accurate. The minister says the report was confidential. But why should a report on the oil fields be so regarded?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
Hear, hear. It cannot
be confidential, it is absurd.
Mr. LeSUEUR: The formation of a policy on a matter of this kind depends on the facts as they exist. Those facts were reported, and it was essential that the House should be made acquainted with them, and should know that previous statements made in this House were accurate. Then the House could adopt what policy it pleased, and continue or eliminate the bounty as it saw fit. I think the House was entitled to the facts. The investigations in question were made by the government at the country's expense, and I think we are entitled to have his report. We are entitled to know what the conditions are in those oil fields and then we can take such action as the circumstances call for. In any event it was improper to have said in an official return that there was no report because the minister has admitted that there was a report, but that it is confidential.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
There comes to the department any number of reports of a confidential character that are not requested to come in that way, that are not intended for the use of parliament. There is a vast difference between these reports. We deal with so many and so varied subjects that my hon. friend may be excused for putting
Supply-Mines

this in the wrong category. We have to get confidential information, and confidential information that we get for the purpose of advising ourselves may take on a vastly different character if made public. I understand that Dr. Hume was sent there on his way westward. He did not come back to make any report on this matter, but he wrote to his deputy minister a short letter of a confidential character which now, it develops, he showed to the gentleman mentioned in the letter whose name I have forgotten. I am perfectly willing to accept the statement. If that is the case, it is absolutely news to me. Of course, the report could be no longer confidential. It was public property; he knew it, and in all probability he saw that information in my office. I do not deny that, but I have always treated that report as one for our own information in the department. In view of what my hon. friend has brought out, I am perfectly willing to lay the report on the table of the House and to treat it no longer as confidential. But I would want it understood that I am at liberty to get confidential reports in the department for my information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
The hon. member for
West Lambton (Mr. LeSueur) has certainly, more by accident than anything else, exposed this afternoon what is a too-common practice on the part of this government;. Whenever anything comes out of a public nature which the government would prefer not to be known, it immediately becomes in the eyes of the government confidential; only that can be published which pleases the eyes of the government. In the first place, if one has to assume that the government has a right to regard as confidential the report of an official on a public question, obtained at public expense, a question that has been debated in parliament. This return is absolutely false, and it is brought down on the minister's authority. This return says that the official made no report; that he was not asked to make a report and that he was not going to. Does the minister suggest that is the truth? It is a deception of parliament. If it had not been that an outsider saw that report, parliament would never have known differently. Certainly the department stands in a most unenviable position in relation to this matter. But this report cannot be confidential. Certainly a government has a right to confidential reports on subjects with respect to which there would be danger in divulging information, danger, for instance, in letting other countries know, communications between ministers of other countries and those of Canada. But to say 
that the government can call a report of one of its own officials on a public question confidential, is ridiculous. What can there be secret? What should in the public interest be secret with relation to the facts in the oil fields in the county of Lambton? The thing is absurd. This man is paid a salary by this country, and1 we are entitled to the full results of his work. He brings in a report. I do not know what was in it, but the presumption is very clear, namely, that it reflects on government policy. The government immediately put their stamp "confidential" on it and, not content with that, they bring a return down to the House stating that the man made no report at all, and further than that, that he is not going to make any; whereas the facts are absolutely the contrary. This is not the first time that something of this kind has occurred. Almost every return brought down by this government bears on the face of it evidence that it is only partly revealing the whole facts. This return reveals nothing. It reveals a letter written to Dr. Hume, but it shows nothing in the world in relation to the results of a trip in respect of which he was given some thousands of dollars of the money of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Of course it would.
What right has the minister or any officer of his department to instruct an officer on salary by this country to go out and investigate a 208
question of public concern and make a private report that the public who are paying him have no right to see? He has no right to do that at all. Before the minister lean be justified in asserting that any document is confidential, he must show that it would be injurious to the country to reveal it at the time. I recall that in the days of the late government, only in connection with correspondence with the United States government and the British government were we compelled to take that stand. We were roundly -and foolishly-abused. In a case of that kind I would never in the world complain. But what harm could there be in submitting the report of an officer on the condition of the oil industry in Lamlbton? There could not possibly be any reason to justify the suppression of it. But he was not asked to suppress it or to make a private report. The instructions are given in a letter to the following effect:
On your way to .and from the field you will spend a few days in the oil fields of southwest Ontario in Kent and Lambton counties with a view to becoming familiar with present conditions in these fields and arranging for closer co-operation with the drilling companies to obtain information regarding the well logs, et<S.
He was to make an investigation there so that the department might become more familiar with the situation; and whatever report he made, whether as a letter or in any other form, is public property from the beginning. Effect Anticipated by Operators by Removed of Bounty
On account of the fact that most of the producers now operate at a loss without the bounty the effect of the removal of the bounty will be a cessation of operations by the operators losing money. Even supposing only a few closed down at once the results are likely to be disastrous because,
1.	A great deal of water is pumped with the oil and this water must be removed before the oil can be obtained. The closing down by a few operators will throw this burden on the remaining operators, which of course, will at once increase production costs and undoubtedly cause others to close down, even though under present conditions they may be operating at a small profit.
2.	The effect of several operators closing down will be to increase the water troubles in the field and flooding will result. The effect of flooding is to permanently destroy the field so that even if the price of oil does increase at a later date operators who were forced to close down will not be able to resume operations. This, I think, is one, if not the most serious, effect on the future of this area as an oil producer.
3.	The effect of decreased production in this area will be to cause the Imperial Oil Company to shut down their receiving stations, now maintained in this area, and to abandon their pipe line which carries the oil to Sarnia. The oil operators left in the field will thus be forced to transport their oil to Sarnia or some other refinery thus increasing their production costs. This, no doubt, would be most serious.
Conclusions.

The effect of the conditions outlined above leaves little doubt that with the withdrawal of the bounty the oil fields of this area will be speedily abandoned and, I take it, this also applies to the other fields in this part of Ontario. This will have a disastrous effect, as far as I can see, on the towns in this area, who have assumed obligations for debentures of a large amount. Debentures were issued in the towns of Petrolia and Oil Springs to cover cost of installing hydro power which is almost universally used in the oil area by the operators for the production of oil and which account for by far the greater part of the power used. Also in Petrolia there are at present at least two machine shops-Mackenzie's and Bain's-each employing a number of men and these are entirely dependent on the oil industry. If a partial or complete cessation of production in this area should result from the withdrawal of the bounty, these industries would be seriously affected and the reduction in population resulting from these and the oil operations themselves would make it extremely difficult for these towns to meet their debenture obligations.
Are the Oil Fields Worth Saving?
There seems no doubt that even under satisfactory conditions to operators for production of oil in this area, the Ontario fields will show a gradual decline in future years but from operators here I have arrived at the conclusion that the decline is likely to be slow. For example Mr. Kerr, a large operator claims his property pumped as much oil in 1923 as it did in 1914 and Mr. J. P. Watt who controls 24 acres and operates 32 wells in Petrolia claims his production is larger than in 1916. There seems reason, therefore, to expect with continuous operation Oil Springs, Petrolia and Enniskillen Township areas will continue to produce much the same quantity of oil as formerly for a number of years and this conclusion is substantiated by the production in barrels shown for the last few years.

Is such a report to be concealed from a Canadian public? What harm could be done by the publicity of that report? What harm could be done to the1 taxpayer of Canada, the people of Canada? None could be suggested. No man however imaginative could suggest the Slightest injury. Consequently, no person can be justified for a moment in suggesting that this report is 'confidential. It would not matter if it were marked confidential in every line-even if at the top or bottom or anywhere in it, it were marked 'Confidential, private, personal or in any other way. I wonder what trust parliament is going to place in the returns of this government after this? I do not think it will plaice very much. As to the merits of the claim for bounty, that is another issue altogether. The total appropriation is $375,000. The items are:
Entomological branch	 $220,000
Experimental farm (Division of Botany) 155,000
Then we have a further subdivision of the vote. The two causes which led to this increase are, first, the increased activities out in the west in connection with the problem of rust, the endeavour to find a rust-proof wheat, or otherwise dealing with the rust problem in some manner that will reduce as far as possible these ravages. This has necessitated the construction of a laboratory at Winnipeg in conjunction with the college in that province. This was partly taken care of last year by a vote for that purpose, and the balance will be taken care of by this vote. The proposition is to put up a fumigating and inspection plant in the city of Montreal to inspect or fumigate certain plant products and such other commodities as require fumigating. This is the result of a new regulation that has been adopted in the United States. A law was recently put on their statutes to provide for the inspection of all plants going into the United States, and as we had a working arrangement with the United States, in order to continue our trade with that country the necessity was imposed upon us of bringing down a similar provision that all shrubs and bulbs coming into Canada would have to be inspected. At the same time this will prevent contagion and will provide the necessary supervision to continue the trade backward and forward between Canada and the United States. We have taken this initial step to provide for this inspection and fumigating plant in the city of Montreal. In addition to this, we intend to use it for fumigating embargoed cargoes that still persist in coming into the country, packed in straw. The House has heard from various members, particularly the hon. member from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), whose case I think we have been able to look after all right, because we had a fumigating plant at Vancouver sufficient to take care of the goods after they had been reduced down to about 20 per cent of what they were last January, by our pro-

Supply-Agriculture
hibitory law. They still come in but not in such quantities that the plant at Vancouver cannot now take care of them. We need a plant at Montreal, and we are going to combine it for these three purposes, shrubs, bulbs and other commodities, and occasionally other cargoes that come in packed in straw. The increase is due to these two causes.

This is a very large vote, and I would not like to reduce it one dollar, if I thought the money was being spent to advantage. As the years pass and the country gets older we find the damage by pests of all kinds is increasing rapidly. Man is able to handle beasts of prey, lions, tigers and those animals that perhaps create a terror in the minds of man, but after all the real danger to humanity to-day is the insect pest. I suppose most hon. members have read about it, and have an idea what it means. If we have no system of combating the insect pest I have no hesitation in saying that in a short time man will be unable to live on this globe which we now inhabit.
It is all right enough for hon. gentlemen to laugh, but it is a very serious matter. Coming down to what we are more familiar with, farm life and growing of crops, we know that the pests are increasing. Out west, when we first began to grow wheat, we had no pests. Now I could name them by almost the dozen. One thing after another comes along, and we are trying to discover some method of combating not only the insect pest but fungi, such as rust. As I said in opening, I would not like to cut down the grant in any way provided the money be spent to the best advantage. We have this trouble with fruit, with trees and with the foliage, and all kinds of crops. This pest of rust means millions of dollars of loss to the wheat crops of Canada. I would like Some information as to what is beinsr done in regard to an investigation in the matter of rust. Is there any increase in the knowledge of how rust damages the wheat or where it comes from? I have listened to a great many addresses and talks about rust, but I have never heard anything to lead me to believe that we are on the way to some discovery which will combat this disease which threatens our agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am very glad to welcome my hon. friend as a doubting lieutenant in this crusade against rust, and not only against rust but against all forms of insect pest and fungi, fungus diseases, because we have come to an age when it is a fight between man and the insect pest. That will 209
be our next great war, and we are right into it now. Let us examine for the moment the remarkable extension of the activities of the corn-borer in Essex, Kent and adjoining counties. It has increased from five hundred to a thousand per cent in its activities this last year, at a time when the people were beginning to think it was about exterminated. The old-fashioned potato bug has caused a complete embargo on our potatoes going into Great Britain. The high tariff of the United States stopped our potatoes going in there, and something else stopped them from going to Cuba, with the result that we have no country to which we can send our potatoes, and one of the causes is the potato bug. In British Columbia we have the fire blight which attacks apples and pears particularly, and in Australia they have placed an embargo against fruit of that class from Canada. I think the embargo was improperly placed, but it is there. All across the continent, from one end to the other, we have pests of this kind, so that in the last two decades there have been no less than seventy-two pieces of legislation, regulation and embargo, passed by the parliament of Canada against goods from other countries, and those countries in turn have passed legislation against imports from Canada, for similar reasons. So that hon. gentlemen will see that the very continuity of our trade depends upon keeping our products free from insect and fungus pests. This fact cannot be too strongly impressed upon the committee. The matter of bugs and bacteria has been made the occasion of a legitimate amount of jest, and we take advantage of it and regard it as a joke. To the man who has had his grain crop attacked by rust two or three years in succession, the thing is no joke. Ask the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) if it was a joke when the land was almost covered with grasshoppers through southern Saskatchewan and into Manitoba and Alberta. Had nature not come to the relief of the provincial government and the municipalities in the shape of a parasite these grasshoppers would not have been rounded up as quickly as they were. Last year the committee on Agriculture, after hearing Professor Gussow's very excellent address on the tremendous annual losses Canada sustains as a result of cereal diseases, including rust, recommended to the House that 850,000 be expended in the launching of a vigorous campaign against these plagues. Last year $25,000 was appropriated for this purpose, most of which was spent on equipment for the new laboratory. Last Sep-

Supply

Agriculture

tember Dr. Grisdale, representing the department, and Dr. Tory, representing the Research Council, invited a number of gentlemen interested in this investigatory work both in the United States and Canada to an international rust conference at Winnipeg, and there the foundation was laid of a strong campaign on the part of both countries against these diseases. Since then there have been several meetings of the sub-committee that was appointed, and Dr. Tory, Dr. Grisdale and Dr. Murray have gone down to the United States looking for the very best men who could be found to deal with the question of fungus diseases, because we have not got in Canada a sufficient number of trained experts to take care of this work. We entered into an agreement with the college authorities of Manitoba under which as their contribution to these activities there should be set apart twenty-five acres of land close to the college buildings, with provision of heat, power and light, the federal government to supply the building and equipment.
What is the estimated cost of the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
About S40.000, including equipment. In January last the authorities of the Dominion, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan met to lay out this work. While we wanted to proceed in cooperation with the United States authorities, we constantly reporting to them and they to us, it was felt that we should have a specific plan for Canada and that certain matters should be delegated to the Winnipeg authorities, certain others to the laboratory authorities at Saskatoon, others to Alberta and others to the Central farm at Ottawa, so that we would have the work going along concurrently at. these four points, with the central activity at Winnipeg. A good many theories have been advanced as to the cause of rust. It is known that some varieties of wheat are immune to it while others are quite susceptible. The old Scott wheat was comparatively immune, while the Clawson wheat was susceptible to it. Twelve or fifteen years ago the idea was conceived of developing a wheat plant that would be immune from rust. During the past ten years more has been learned about rust than has been learned in the preceding two hundred years, in searching about for a plant that would be immune. It has been found that there are no less than thirty-nine different species of rust, and that some varieties of wheat are immune from some of the rust species but not from others. It was thought by some that the barberry bush 
was the primary cause of the rust; that it acted as a host plant for the rust spore. It has since been discovered by experiment that these spores are carried in the upper currents of the atmosphere, usually from south to north, starting with the early ripening wheat in Texas and proceeding northward through Kansas, the Dakotas and Minnesota, and thence into Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and now to some extent in Alberta. On a calm day these spores, having been carried in the upper currents, are precipitated on the crop. A calm, murky day, with intermittent sunshine and rain, is what we call a ibad rust day.
Mr. FORKE. I doubt it. When we have had a bad attack of rust it has usually followed extreme heat.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
If you have a
period of drought lasting three or four weeks the plant is weakened, and then when there is just enough moisture to make the rust spores develop they commence to drive their activities home on the plant. If you have it bright, fair, dry and cold, the danger from rust is not so great; it is warm enough for the growth of the wheat but too cold to encourage the rapid development of the rust. For the most -part it is a question of a neck-and-neck race. As a matter of fact, it has proved to be a neck-andLneck race. Had it been a little warmer, a little moister, a little calmer, the rust would have developed. That is the theory, and that is as far as we have got-ns far as I have got at all events. I had the privilege of meeting some of the very best experts of the United States who had made a life study of this problem, and they are all of the one mind, that one of the most fruitful sources of contagion is through the upper currents of the atmosphere, running three and four miles high and then quietly dropping. Now how are we going to ward that off? We cannot put an umbrella over the country and ward it off. We can do something practical in eradicating the barberry bush, and there is a campaign all over the United States, in every wheat state, to eradicate the barberry bush. A regular survey is being made of the country, and everywhere the barberry bush is found they go after it. That is one thing we can control, but there is no way of controlling the winds, and the waves, if you like to put it that way. Man has no dominion over the winds, especially the upper currents. I suppose some of the flying men have found that out, although they have pretty well navigated the upper currents.

Supply-Agriculture
The only way to meet the difficulty is to have a rust-resisting plant developed. Any wheat that will ripen more early is more resistant to rust. Marquis wheat is more resistant. It crosses the line before the rust can get after it, and the binder is cutting. Then we have that newer wheat, Garnet, a very good wheat, which is some eight or nine days earlier. Even if it were not more resistant than Marquis, the fact that it is some eight days earlier puts it in the running.

Does not the minister think
there is a possibility of the rust starting right down at the gulf of Mexico and coming up with the wheat crop as it gradually ripens?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Chairman, that that is along the line of the investigational work. Those are the sources of contagion known so far, and they are confirmed by the best investigators who have made a life study of this problem in the United States. At the conference at Winnipeg, these experts were very pronounced on these two sources of contagion, and were exceedingly insistent that we should pursue our campaign against the buckthorn and the barberry, because that came within our powers. Whenever you see the barberry bush adjacent to a wheat field, you will see lots of rust in the immediate vicinity. Other sources of contagion may be discovered, and experts are working on the different breeds. Kota wheat, while not as good as some of the others is resistant to some varieties of spores, but not co them all. That is the stage, roughly speaking, where the investigation is at the present time.

We all appreciate the fact
that the minister is doing what he can to fight ravages of insect pests, including rust. As one who 'has had practical experience of its ravages, I wish to express my appreciation of the attempt, at least, of the government to find some solution for this problem.
Now I would like to get back to the financial end. This matter was up for discussion in the committee on Agriculture, and I think the deputy minister gave us the information that the government contemplated erecting in Winnipeg, on the Agricultural College site, a laboratory building in connection with this work. I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to go on with this building, what is the probable cost, and if they have made any arrangement with the Manitoba government, and if so, whether the 209}
Manitoba government have agreed to the arrangement made.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think my hon.
friend could not have been in when I gave that information. I gave that before, as I thought it was the first information I should give. We have an agreement, signed and delivered, whereby the Manitoba government, through the College of Agriculture, supplies the land, the heat, power and light, while this government supplies the building and equipment. About $15,000 of last year's vote was devoted to equipment. We could not build in the winter, but we could buy the equipment. About $25,000 of this increase goes to put up the laboratory, and the $15,000 of equipment is ready to move in. The other $25,000 goes to another laboratory for a similar purpose in the city of Montreal.

I listened to the discussion, but I wanted it brought out distinctly whether or not the Manitoba government had agreed to this. The minister says they have agreed to it. I have it upon good authority that they have not agreed to the proposition, but that is by the way.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
What is my hon.
friend's authority for that?

I have it 'here, and I can
give it to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There was a while
when the matter was referred from the president of the college and the president of the university to the government for confirmation, and the Premier of Manitoba drew attention to certain changes he desired, and these changes were covered by a communication from myself. So far as I know it is satisfactory. It is not material anyway; we are going ahead anyhow; we have an arrangement made.

In view of the fact that we have in Manitoba a plant that cost approximately $4,000,000, not a cent of which has ever been paid-we have borrowed the money and are paying interest on it still-in view also of the fact that that plant is being utilized to only about one-half of its capacity, because although every building may be utilized for some specific purpose, they are being utilized to only one-half their capacity, I think it is a serious thing for this government or the Manitoba government to contemplate any additional expenditure for extensions to the buildings we have there now. Unless the government have made all possible investigations and have found they cannot get out
Supply-Agriculture

of putting up that building, I would say to them to-night in all earnestness that they should make every attempt to see if they cannot utilize some of the buildings already there for this worthy purpose. I am heartily in accord with the work that is to be done. I wish to see it go on, and I would not be niggardly in appropriating money for this work, because it is very important work, but I would hesitate spending more public money for buildings in Winnipeg when we have already $4,000,000 tied up in buildings now, not one dollar of which has been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We tried hard to get a little corner of that S4.000,000, but we could not, We went into it thoroughly with President McLean and President McKillican, of the Agricultural college. They have a very fine laboratory there, but it is practically all in use at the present time, and if we went in there as well we would be simply crowding each other, and that would not be a very good start for harmonious team play between two governments; it would be like a team of horses each crowding for the road, and my hon. friend knows they do not go very good that way. Then we tried to get an adjoining building, the mechanical building. W'e tried every way, and hesitated a long while because we wanted to have good equipment, but finally we were driven to the conclusion that there was only one way, and that was to put up a new building. There was no building and in such a situation as this the necessary thing is to get the land and the buildings close together. They would not let us have it under any consideration whatever, and yet it is necessary that the land should be adjacent to the building for the convenience of the work. I can assure my hon. friend that we felt and the Manitoba government felt just as strongly, the desirability of not incurring any unnecessary expense. They are quite as conscious as anybody can be that they have got all the money they want invested in buildings, and they were quite generous in their views as to the disposition of the land for this purpose, and for the provision of heat, power and light. Now an arrangement has been entered into that when we come to dissolve partnership there will be a suitable settlement arrived at.

I understand that the arrangement has not been agreed to by the Manitoba government either, but I wish to stress this fact: Notwithstanding that we have this mammoth plant in Manitoba, and similar plants all over the Dominion, there is a desire for further building to carry on this work. I
	-
do not believe the members of the House begin to appreciate the amount of money that we have got tied up in public buildings in this country. On this subject I should like to read an extract from the Manitoba Free Press. This is from an interview given by the agricultural experts from the Old Country who toured this country last year. It is a short extract which is very appropriate to the subject and I will read it. It will go to show what they think of our elaborate plants in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Whose opinion is my hon. friend going to quote?

I am going to quote from an interview given by the British experts who toured Canada last year. This extract is taken from the Manitoba Free Press of September 2, 1924. This is what it says:
All through our tour we have coveted the magnificent agricultural colleges and experimental stations of Canada. The money which has been expended on any one agricultural college in Canada is many times greater than that expended on any similar institution in the British Isles, probably more than has been spent in erecting all the similar institutions of Scotland or Ireland, and possibly of England.
Yet we find it necessary, although we have less than one-quarter the population they have, to erect additional buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks he can find a corner in those magnificent buildings in which we can do this work the chances are yet good. We have not started to put up the building; we are just getting the plans out.
Did you try the parliament building?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is reserved for another purpose. We certainly exhausted our energy in searching in every quarter we could to secure a place in which we could do good work. The fact that this is an expensive building does not necessarily imply that there will be a corresponding working space. It is a magnificent building, at least to look at, and one that you can take a pride in. At the same time there is not the room available corresponding at all to its appearance. We were not looking for grand architecture, we wanted a working laboratory, and we now have an agreement with the Manitoba government in which they have concurred. We tried to get into what they call the mechanical building, we tried to get accommodation everywhere we could, before we reached a decision. As a matter of fact we have not started to build yet

I understand the buildings
are to be suitable in every way, and that a large number of hot houses will be needed to carry on this work effectively; is that true?

I do not think there is
any more important work the government can undertake than this particular work. It is a kind of work, I think, that if it is to be done at all must be done properly.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Sure. .

There is simply no use in
attempting to do this work unless it is done well.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Hear, hear.

While none of us like to see more buildings put up than are necessary, yet I can appreciate the fact that this special work requires a particular kind of building, and a somewhat expensive kind of building too.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Hear, hear.

For my part while I would urge the most economical construction possible in this building, I would not like to put a stone in the way of carrying out the proposition that has been entered into for it is most important work that we are engaged in.

May I just add a word
or two. I think it is most important to carry on this work also; I do not want the committee for a moment to imagine I am opposing the work undertaken by the government. But I am protesting against any additional expenditure in public buildings, and I want the fact brought out that either this government or the Manitoba government will be held responsible by the people for this further expenditure on public buildings. If this government claims that it could not get along without this building, that there was nothing suitable already available, it will have to take the blame. An/, if the Manitoba government says "We cannot accommodate you in our buildings, they are for our own private use," they will have to take the blame and the responsibility for their action before the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
After the generous *way in which the committee on Agriculture took hold of this last year, and made the recommendation that $25,000 should be devoted to the desired object, we would have been very remiss in our duty if we did not go forward with this work just as rapidly as we could. We
have done so. We could not get the buildings sought, and we have entered into an agreement with the Manitoba government. That government has agreed' to the arrangement. Oh yes. My hon. friend (Mr. Leader) will have to do more than shake his head. I do not know what he has got there to the contrary. I have written to the Premier of Manitoba and we have an agreement with the authorities of the university. There was a time when the Manitoba government did point to the necessity of some supplementary understanding so -that in the event of our dissolving (partnership there would be a friendly dissolution. I may say further that our working relations with the Manitoba government have been most friendly and cordial from the beginning, and in order to have those relations continue it was necessary to have that thorough understanding and then start out. I think we are in good shape to do good work. May I point -out to my hon. friend that the very fact that we are co-operating with them is another indication that we are trying to cut out unnecessary duplication. We are working in conjunction not only with the government of Manitoba but also with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I think my hon friend is just 'getting -the wrong steer on that question, the wrong slant on it, that is all. He has -got, well a little bit of something to talk about, you know.
I can assure the minister that I have not got-did he say?-a wrong steer. I have got the authority in my hand to establish that the Manitoba government has not yet approved of this.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What date is that?
It is dated March 10, 1925.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh that is quite a while ago.
It is a letter from a private individual, but I have no hesitation in letting the minister see the -signature.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Well, my -goodness, governments I know are proverbially slow but nevertheless there has surelly been time -to adjust the matter since March 10. I will take my hon. friend's word for it that the date is M-arch 10, but just -the same I assure him that there was not -a hitch or a disagreement with the Manitoba authorities. They did think however that there should be a -thorough understanding in the event of a time coming when we thought it desirable to dissolve partnership on the work. However, I accept my hon. friend's statement that the date he speaks of was two months ago.
