10 p,m. ment, that they did not think anything there suited them. Immediately after that I wrote to Winnipeg and received this letter, so the arrangement was not completed on that date, March 10.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Pardon me I do
not want to be like the individual that wants the last word, but is not that two months ago? We are talking of conditions to-day. That was over two months ago.
Yes but I understand you claim an arrangement was made before the deputy minister made his announcement in the committee which was before March 10.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh well!

As one who has been following this proposal very closely I want to say at the outset that I am very pleased indeed to see the co-operative spirit that exists between the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, also the progress towards an international arrangement that has been made with the northern states interested in this same rust problem. I think the parties interested are greatly to be praised for bringing about- this cordial spirit of co-operation in a movement to overcome the dreaded disease known as rust. In regard to the buildings at Winnipeg I understand that a committee of the university met the officers of the federal Department of Agriculture and both parties went to the agricultural college and made a thorough survey. Personally, I was firmly of opinion that space should be -available at that institution to carry on this work. Not being familiar with the technical rpart of this work, I must confess that I have %>een compelled to give way to the opinions of those who have made a study and know something of it. The report of the committee was that it was impossible to get laboratory, greenhouse and field space that could be so arranged at the present time as to carry on the work efficiently. I am convinced that the parties who were looking into this matter were doing so with the intention of doing the best possible in fighting this disease. Consequently, I give way to the officials who have decided that it is impossible to get the proper space. But I feel so strongly on the question that sometimes I would almost like to ask the department, even yet, if it is not too late, to see if it is not possible to get 	i
some space there and not to spend more money than is absolutely essential. I may be wrong. But I have the feeling sometimes that some of our scientific men have a tendency towards extravagance and ask for things just a little more handy than is absolutely necessary for really efficient work. I do not want to hamper the efficiency of the staff in any way, but I should like the government to do the work as cheaply and economically as they possibly can. If the building is not under way yet, I feel so strongly on this that I w'ould almost suggest that a new survey of available space should be made. I am not casting any reflection upon the officers or the committee that looked into this question. I believe they were sincere and anxious to bring about the best possible results and I am going to leave it at that. I am going to give way regarding this question if these scientific men are firmly convinced that it is impossible to carry on the work efficiently in the present buildings. I will not oppose the expenditure for a moment, because it is essential that something be done immediately to combat this disease.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
While we have already had three surveys made for the purpose in view that the hon. member mentions, that is to see if we could not find some of these buildings suitable for the work, one survey being made in September immediately after the international conference when I was there, the next in January and the last in April, in spite of that, I will assure my hon. friend that we shall draw the matter again to Premier Bracken's attention and send him a marked copy of Hansard showing this discussion. If any space is discovered in the meantime, it is not too late, but we must proceed as quickly as possible with the work. You have expected us to do that. Are there any other suggestions, because this is a work which people have been at for years and years, and in my estimation, we are only in the a-b-c of it. I- am not beguiled by the thought that we are going to solve this problem in a year. It may take five years or it may take twenty-five years. This committee is aware of the research work that has been done during the last twenty-five years in regard to the eradication of tuberculosis. There is still something to be done that will immunize animals and mankind too from the ravages of this disease. Those who are doing this work are getting hotter, as the saying is. They are coming to know more about it. No man, however, can tell yet what may be accomplished. All we know is that there is

Supply-Agriculture
sufficient persistence in man to surmount this difficulty in time.

Provided that no suitable
building is discovered at the college or in the city of Winnipeg, is it the intention of the department to go ahead with the new building this season?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes. The land is secured and the plans are all prepared1.
The minister asks for suggestions. I would suggest that we have a university at Saskatoon where suitable buildings might be found.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Some of the work is being done there by Mr. Fraser, a very good man. He has associates there, and he is doing the work under the supervision of President Murray who is so intensely interested in it that he went down into the United States to help us to hunt three good men for the work.

I appreciate the importance of carrying on this work, but at the same time I wish to add my protest to that of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). The Dominion seems top-heavy with public buildings from one end to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What is the particular protest now?
That we should not go on with this building on th.e campus of the university at Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Where should we
put it?

I believe we could have
found room at Saskatoon. I do not believe it is necessary that this work should be carried on at Winnipeg. We have at Saskatoon many public buildings that I do not think are overcrowded at all, and we could have found room there. The work will be temporary to a large extent, and I am inclined to think, if we are going to find a remedy at all, we shall do so very soon. We are spending rather too much money in bricks and mortar throughout the Dominion in the present financial state of this country. With all the empty buildings that there are in the cities we could have found room for this work without putting up another building costing as much as it is expected to cost.

I checked some of the details although I had not time to go into the matter very closely. But I was interested to find if possible some reason for the excessive expenditure and I discovered, for example, that at one experimental farm there were two men whose travelling expenses, although their per diem allowance was the same, differed considerably.
I have not the details before me, but speaking from memory I should say that one man for a lesser number of days had double the amount of travelling expenses. I found the same sort of thing in several instances, and I think that we may fairly assume that the / man with the lower expense account is a good official who is careful of the public's money. The man who has an inordinate travelling expense account, with the same per diem allowance, although he does not travel the same number of days, certainly is not so good an official, or at any rate the indication is that there is some laxity. This magnificent vote is given without any grudge to agriculture year after year because, I think, the whole country is anxious to promote the work that

is done and is ready to give it general support. But when we find an item of $866,000 in one year for travelling expenses, exclusive of the cost of a large number of automobiles and so on, then I say that there is something that evidently merits very careful consideration.
There should be a strict investigation on the part of the minister or on the part of competent officials in his department into the whole question. A first class accountant, one of his own staff, might be directed to check up this class of expenditure. I know that the minister is an exceedingly busy man, and all that is necessary in the circumstances is to call this abnormal expenditure to his attention to have this extravagance curtailed.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: I hope the minister will accept my criticism as he did a moment ago, in good part.

The case I mentioned was not in an expensive city. I do not want to mention any names, because I have no desire to drag the officials into this House. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
These remarks are quite all right, and as a matter of fact we are doing that very thing now in one or two cases which I am sorry to have to look into. With regard to assigning a multiplicity of duties to one man, this is being done in some cases.

I question whether we can do that in that department, but we can do it where conditions lend themselves to it. Take the case of the egg inspectors; we have so few of them in comparison with the extent of the country that they are on the hop, skip and jump continuously and it takes them all their time to go after old Biddy and her chicks. I do not think we can add anything to their duties. But wherever it can be done it is being done. In the Seed branch now there is such a great amount of work we wonder where they would come in on this proposition. They are working with the additional load without the additional salary. We have been asked to raise their salaries, owing to the multiplicity of their duties. However, anybody who has endeavoured to obtain reclassification from the Civil Service Commission knows that he has a job ahead of him. In the main we are working along the lines indicated. agreeable to it if the money was spent in Saskatoon. I do not know whether he is exactly consistent in the position he takes.

there.

No, not for that building.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Then the hon.
gentleman does not want it at Saskatoon. Well, all right, we understand it. I am afraid my hon. friend wants to have his eye both ways, first on the treasury and then on his constituency. Well, there is no harm in that.

Let me put the minister
right. I protested against the construction of a new building, and I said I thought room could be found without constructing any building.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Then my hon.
friend did not want it at Saskatoon.

Is any portion of this
money to be spent in fumigating plants in the Maritime provinces?

I believe there
should be. We have one building at St. John at the present time. John.

I wish to say a word on
behalf of the minister and his estimates.
Supply-Agriculture

I recollect well that in the committee on Agriculture we listened to an able address on the question of rust by Dr. Gussow, and an animated discussion immediately followed the address. I might state that I liked that address much better than I liked the address on hog raising.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not think much of the address on hog raising.

But after the animated discussion before the committee on Agriculture last year, we made a unanimous request for a grant of $50,000 for the commencement of the construction of the plant for investigational purposes in regard to rust. When we suffer $90,000,000 damage per year from the ravages of rust, surely hon. gentlemen in this chamber cannot very well criticize an expenditure of $25,000 voted last year, which was only one-half thp amount asked for, and one-fourth of the amount which Dr. Gussow recommended, namely $100,000. I think we are just a little too earnest in the application of economy. In my opinion that is false economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Because it is a fact we have been losing the wealth of this country to the extent of $90,000,000 a year through the ravages of rust, and the Dominion government at last is waking up to the enormity of this thing and is working in co-operation with the United States Department of Agriculture and in co-operation with the provinces, and probably in the near future we will reach a solution. When we asked for $50,000 last year I understood it was to provide a hothouse, in which to carry on experiments with the barberry bush, which serves as a host plant for the rust germ, and in which scientists could follow the activities of the rust germ particularly through the winter season, something that- up to the present time in Canada they have not been able to do. Now if it is necessary to spend money to provide these facilities, I think it is altogether wrong and false economy to suggest that the expenditure should be spread over three or four years, because if the money were spent pt the present time the trouble could be overcome. It is wise to expend it in the first place, and then in the years to come we will hope to lose less than $90,000 000 a year. I rise to support the vote, I accept the word of the minister that they have done all they can, and I realize that in using Winnipeg as the location more facilities are offered for the professors at. the universities to the south to come in 
and confer with them, whereas Saskatoon is much further away and more expense would be involved if the experimental plant were located there. I did make a recommendation to the minister in regard to this matter. Arrangements have been made with the University of Manitoba, and the preliminary work is being commenced there. The minister may be sure I will always support any reasonable expenditure for the investigation of rust and insect pests in this country.

I would be the last to
protest against any expenditure on behalf of the agriculturists of this country, but one cannot help being startled at the expenditure of $866,000 in one year on travelling expenses in one department. I believe there are 420 employees, which would make an average of over $2,000 each for travelling expenses in the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The 420 are the
employees in Ottawa. There are about 1,600 all told.

Even at that we have
about $500 each for travelling. At any rate, $866,000 is a startling figure. Perhaps I owe an apology to gentlemen I criticized for making a trip to Wembley. I remember the chief whip of the Liberal party was very severe in his criticisms of one minister who spent $10.000, or nearly that, on a trip overseas with his secretaries, but this amount of nearly a million in one department makes these other expenditures look like shadow-boxing in comparison. It seems to me the minister could in this respect save some thousands of dollars, without reduction of efficiency, to the people who are already severely burdened with taxation. I cannot help thinking that a great deal of this $866,000 was unnecessarily expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Can my hon. friend point to where it could be cut down?

That is not my business;
it is for the minister to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The work of this
department is largely educational and must be done for the most part through travelling by members of the staff. The travelling expense is one-seventh of the whole expenditure of the department, and I am surprised it is not more. There is need, of course, for careful supervision, and I think it has got it. My hon. friend's feelings in the matter, as one who has not had any experience in administering affairs relating to agriculture, are easily understood. Anyone not knowing anything about it would think just as he does.

Supply-Agriculture

What progress has been
made in the control of the codling moth? I understand that in British Columbia that control is shared between the provincial and the Dominion governments; is that the case in the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have been fumigating cars, banding trees, spraying, and taking other steps to circumscribe the activities of this moth. Every country is protecting itself against the invasion of these noxious insects, therefore it behooves us to be alert in their suppression, and, if possible, their extermination. As to the sharing of the control, that depends on the province. Some provinces will take hold of it and others will not. In every province, however, steps are being -taken to eradicate this pest.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Publications, $18,500.

I think the department might well cust down on some of these publications. I know they send out a list so that persons interested imay indicate the publications they desire, and that is a wise thing to do, but I -cannot help thinking -that we are spending too much money on publications that are seldom or nev-er read.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Formerly there was an indiscriminate distribution of this kind of literature, but that is not done now. The publications are sent out only on application.
Are there no -publications sent out by the Agriculture department except on request?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
Is any information given in these publications regarding experiments with sugar beets such as have been carried on at Winnipeg by -this new firm which has offered -to distribute seed from Germany
for the sugar beet industry? Can any of that seed be obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I remember having some correspondence with my colleague the Minister of National Defence with regard to certain c'ubs organized in the Maritime provinces, to whose members the Central farm distributes beet seed. The request was made that these clubs be increased in membership from a possible fifty to a possible one hundred.
Would that be the same seed as is used in Germany?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. This is Ontario grown seed. In addition to that we analyse the beets, so as to keep them in the direction of growing the highest quality of beets.

I suppose the
minister is aware that this company in Winnipeg is distributing beet seed.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is a private company.
Is it distributing a different class of seed altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We distribute Ontario grown seed, but, of course, originally most of this seed was imported. I think some of the Winnipeg seed is imported.
Does the minister think the beets test out as good for sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The Ontario grown seed produces a higher testing beet than the seed we have been importing.

Due to the mild criticism that I offered of this vote a few minutes ago, I do want after looking the matter over, to commend the minister for having cut this down $15,000 from last year. How much was spent under this head last year, and was the reduction due to the fact that you were not spending as much, or because you were cutting down the publications?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This vote is for distribution, and the cost is borne by the respective branches.

This does not include
the printing?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No. The reduction is due to the fact that we have no longer got the expense of distributing the Agricultural Gazette. Formerly that was not only distributed but printed out of this vote.
Supply-Agriculture

Am I to understand
that it costs $18,500 merely to distribute these pamphlets? Is that postage, or are they delivered by special messenger, or how?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend the cost of the different items. First, there is the cost of advertising our publications. Sometimes when we have anything new to send out we put a very small ad in our farm papers, and that results in requests for the publication. Envelopes alone cost $8,000, labour $3,GD0, 'equipment and maintenance $2,000, postage, express and cartage $2,000, printing and stationary $2,500.

How many envelopes
would there be in that $8,OGO? I do not want to be picayune, but $8,000 is an enormous sum for cheap manilla envelopes.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I understand this
would cover several millions of envelopes.

Are envelopes used in
practically every case? The Department of Labour have adopted, not an envelope, but the publication is rolled up and pasted at one end with a little strip of mucilage. That would cost I should think one-quarter of what the envelopes would cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have not used that.

To what extent are
applications being made for these publications, in Ontario, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I understand that
in Ontario the applications will run up to about half a million. It depends upon how much we advertise. If we put a small notice in the farm press indicating a number of bulletins that are available, we generally find a run on those afterwards. We have not very much money for advertising, and when you limit the advertising, the demand is less. If we spent more in advertising, the chances are the demand would be greater; so it just depends what you are seeking. I do not think we have done much advertising of any kind lately for the simple reason that we have not the money.

Over and above that,
is there a mailing list for all Canada to whom you send each one of these publications?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is no recognized mailing list except for t/he publication we call Seasonable Hints, but if a request comes in for the bulletins that are issued on vegetables, gardening, or anything like that,

these would be sent. But there is no regular mailing list except for Seasonable Hints.

There are lists of the
department's publications sent out to individuals, and they are asked to mark an X opposite the publications they wish mailed to them during the year. You must have some mailing list for taking care of these requests.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They go out in
the same envelope with Seasonable Hints.

Do I understand that
$18,500 is for the purpose of distribution only, or does it include also the cost of printing?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Just for distribution.

According to the Auditor
General's report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1924, page 879, the disbursements on publications amount to $28,500. Of that amount the King's Printer, for printing, receives $17,235.97. Apparently 60 per cent of the vote went for printing. Now if the minister claims, as he does claim, that the item of $18,500 does not include printing, surely there must be an excess in expenditure in the other items as compared with the fiscal year 1923-1924.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is obvious we
could not get those into the public accounts of a year or two ago. What other year is my hon. friend referring to? Last year? Well, the publication of the Agricultural Gazette, as intimated a moment ago, was charged to this account in addition to the distribution. Now we are not publishing it, and next year's vote will not show any item in that regard.

Under what vote will
the publication of the Agricultural Gazette appear this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We are not publishing it.
You are not publishing it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No it has been
dropped.

If I understand the minister correctly he says that the elimination of the publication of the Agricultural Gazette is responsible for the reduction of this vote; but in the Auditor General's report for 192324 the principal items, apart from the printing of the Agricultural Gazette, are stationery,

Supply-Agriculture
$4,000 odd and wages and labour $4,000 odd, amounting to between eight and nine thousand dollars. The others are aid insignificant items. Now this vote is double that amount, and surely it cannot be for distribution purposes only. A short time ago the minister said that certain items, I did not quite catch the amount, were to cover postage and express charges. I fail to see why the department has to pay postage on periodicals or pamphlets that are mailed out. They certainly must go through the mails free as all publication emanating from the departments do.

Shall
the item carry?

Do you not think, Mr. Chairman, I am entitled to a reply to the arguments I have advanced. There must be something else besides the cost of distribution to account for a vote of $18,500, when in the last fiscal year of which we have a record all the various items, apart from printing, only amount to something like $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I can only go over my explanation again if that is what my hon. friend wants. Perhaps the hon. gentleman was not in when I read the itemized account.
I was in my seat.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Then what my hon. friend wants now is to reconcile the difference between this and what appears to be the expenditure for another year. I do not think I am called upon to reconcile the difference. It will be accounted for next year. The activities of the year to which my hon. friend alludes were based upon another vote altogether. One large item of expenditure was the Agricultural Gazette which was a veiy expensive publication. It was printed on very high-class paper and, if I remember rightly, had an expensive cover. I understand from my deputy that it cost about $15,000; I do not know if that includes the cost of distribution or not. Yes, it does include the cost of distribution. So there you have $15,000. That one item alone plus the $18,000 would make $33,500. I do not know what figures my hon. friend wants to harmonize but assuming that I am correct the total of the two amounts would be $33,500.

I think I made it plain
that in the year 1923-24 when the department was publishing or having published the Agricultural Gazette and for which an item appears in the Auditor General's report of $17,235 for the King's printer-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
For the Gazette
alone?
For the Gazette mostly.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It costs a little
more than I said.

-the balance of the vote amounted to less than 810,000. Now, with lessened activities for the year 1925-26 there being a decrease in expenditure of $103,500, we are called upon to vote $10,000 more for distribution, and yet the publication of the Gazette has been eliminated. If the minister wants to reconcile the figures he must show wherein it costs $10,000 more to distribute today the publications of his department when the Agricultural Gazette is not being circulated and the activities of the whole department are less.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You want to know what we are doing with the $17,000 we are saving, is that it?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is what I
understand. We are not publishing the Gazette now. The Gazette cost $17,000 and the amount must be reduced by that sum.
I will try and make it plain this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
If my hon. friend
will just sit down a moment I will explain. We are sending out additional literature to the Wembley exhibition which is going to continue for another year. Last year our vote for distribution was increased because of the extra distribution that was necessary by reason of the Wembley exhibition. This year the distribution of publications at Wembley will continue in greater degree so that there will be that much more for this particular purpose, although the publication of the Gazette has ceased. In other words the fact that there is more business accounts for it.

That is quite right. Had
the minister given the information, when he was first asked, that more publications were being sent to the Wembley exhibition we would have understood why the vote was increased. But to my mind the amount is still too high because when the Gazette was being circulated the distribution cost less than $8,000, and to-day with no Gazette circulated the cost of the distribution of publications amounts to $18,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well it is all right now anyway.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Agriculture
International Institute of Agriculture, $13,500.
Is this vote for the International Institute at Rome

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes. The committee will remember that last year I promised that I would endeavour to consolidate this branch with the main department under the assistant deputy minister. That has been done and it has resulted not only in a small saving in connection with this i'em but also .a saving under the heading of civil government. By that consolidation we have saved one salary and a little bit more, 'but work will be carried on just as before.

I should like to ask if this
vote represents a grant to that institution, or is it intended to cover the expenses of a delegate to Rome?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Part of it is for the
library in the west block. We have a very valuable and a very complete library there. Part is for the usual cost of administration in the way of maintenance and supplies, and the balance is for the maintenance of the offices in Rome where a permanent staff is kept towards the expense of which we
11 p.m. contribute a proportionate share in common with some thirty other countries interested in the same work. Here is how the total of $13,500 is made up: Contribution made towards the maintenance of the International Institute at Rome, $8,900; maintenance of library, binding, stationery, subscriptions, and so forth in Ottawa, $4,600. The cost of the offices at Rome, like every other institution has gone up, as the saying is, since the war, and the result is that we find this part of the expenditure continually growing. On the other hand we have effected a reduction in expenditure through the consolidation which I mentioned.

What other countries
contribute to the upkeep of this institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Nearly every civilized country in Europe that is in the League of Nations.
What do we get in return for this outlay?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We do not get some of the things we thought we were going to get, but on the other hand we get some things more than we bargained for. For instance, we get a little more expense for maintaining the offices. But if you are going to work in conjunction with the nations of the world, whether it be in the League of Nations or

in this kind of a league, some expenditure is necessary.
I realize that you cannot put down in dollars and cents what you get in return; but what service do we get from this institute, and does the minister consider this is money well spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In a few weeks we shall get the complete acreage of the world and statistics of the various cereals. That is compiled and centralized there and it is redistributed throughout the world. Every civilized country is in the League of Nations now and some that are not in the League of Nations are in this. David Lubin was the enthusiast that travelled all over the world with the idea in mind of organizing this institute. I had the pleasure of meeting him, and I was inspired to some extent by his vision of what could Ibe accomplished. In the fall of the year it is worth while knowing where Canada-stands in relation to other countries in the matter of cereal production. We discovered first through that source what our status was. We discovered two years ago authentically that we were the largest wheatexporting country in the world. Statistics are sometimes not as reliable as they might be, but this is a really authentic source of statistics. I have never heard of it being disputed, and I consider for the amount of money we are spending, we get a reasonably good service. I understand that sixty-two countries participate in this activity.

I am going to suggest
to the minister that we have been very-patient and, I think, very moderate with him to-night. The hour is getting late. We sat very- late last night, and I think we have sat very late every night this week except Wednesday when we did not sit at night. I would suggest- that we might adjourn at this late hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I feel so good
natured to-night that I am ready to submit to anything that is requested.

We have submitted to a
good deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Let us finish this
item.

I have followed the
work of the International Institute of Agriculture with a good deal of interest, and I am not as optimistic as to the value we are getting to-day as I was some years ago. For instance, I think the statistics we get are so

Supply-Agriculture
old before we get them they are not of very much benefit to the producer in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We get them very
promptly.
I am quite sure of this statement, that there is a possibility that they are of more benefit to the speculator, let us say in wheat or commodities of that kind, than they are to the producer.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It works both ways.

If this information were made available to the producer so that he might know whether there was a shortage of cereals in the world supply or not, he would know better whether he should sell at the price offered or not. If some method were devised of making this more readily available to the producer or if the information were made available earlier in the season, it might be of more benefit to him. I am not, however, opposing the vote. This institute performs a useful function.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend has a popular misconception of the uses to which it may be put. When the statistics indicate a very large crop, that naturally has the effect of lowering the price. An abundance all over means as a rule lower prices. But when you get the other information, as we did last year, from a reliable source that the crop is quite short, this has the other effect. Up goes the price. The question is one of getting the information in a reliable fashion in this way or in an unreliable way through any other medium. This goes through the press in the regular way.

I have in mind something that happened to us in the potatogrowing section of New Brunswick in 1916, I think it was. It was when the Canada Food board was functioning. I will agree at once with the minister that the reliability of these statistics is all important. In that year a report was issued that there -were to be 28,000,000 bushels of potatoes for export in Canada.. Potatoes were selling in New Brunswick at $2 a barrel out in the field at that time which was in October. We had never exported more than 4,000,000 bushels prior to that. We were selling in the United States and Cuba, the United States market not being closed then by the Fordney duties. This had such a disturbing effect, that the wholesalers in the countries in which we were selling, believing we had such an abnormal crop for export, immediately dropped the price. They would not buy except for present requirements.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It was not the
institute that got out that report.

No. The Canada Food board. I am speaking of the reliability of the statistics. Immediately after the report was issued, the price dropped to $1.50 a ban-el, and within three weeks it went down to 80 cents and it continued so during the whole winter. Instead of exporting 28,000,000 bushels, we exported the usual quantity of 4,000,000 bushels, and there was a shortage in other places with the result that in April, after the New Brunswick crop was all sold, the price rose to as high as $7 a barrel because there were none to be had. That year I claim-and I have made this statement more than once in this House-that they beat the potato producers in New Brunswick out of a profitable price for their potatoes. It cost about $1.50 a barrel to grow them in New Brunswick and the price was 80 cents a barrel. If that report had not been issued, potatoes would have been selling at $2 a barrel. Our supply ran short in March and we did not have enough to supply the market during the shortage in other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Is that not an argument in favour of getting information through a really reliable source?

Yes. But I think we
should be absolutely sure of the reliability before the statistics are published. That report did us more damage in New Brunswick than we have recovered from since.

Has this item anj
connection with a vote passed this afternoon in regard to the grant to the Imperial Institute? That was in the estimates of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart).

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It has no connection. Each department runs its own show.

In the co-ordinating of
these two departments, how many employees has the minister been able to let out?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Three altogether,
the director and two of the staff. We are retaining the librarian and three others, and the work is all under the assistant deputy minister.

Was the minister able
by this to let out the institute commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, but that comes out of civil government. It does not show in this reduction.
Supply-A gricul ture
Was he giving satisfaction, or was he let out because he was not giving satisfaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I could give two or three reasons that would all be true, but the principal reason is that there was never any necessity for a branch there at all as far as I could see. As in some other cases, it was established for the purpose of giving someone a position. There was no justification for a separate. branch.
That is reason enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I promised the
committee last j'ear that I would try to consolidate the work, and this I am endeavouring to do all along the line.
Is not the institute largely a statistical organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.
Why should it not be linked up with the Bureau of Statistics? It would seem to be a wise thing to have all the statistical branches of the government together.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I discussed the
matter with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), but if I handed the work over to him it would inflate his expenses. It was discussed just before we were preparing the estimates and we decided to let it stay as it was. Of course, all information in regard to agriculture as well as other industries, so far as exports are concerned, is compiled through the Department of Trade and Commerce. That is where the director of this institute gets his information for transmission to Rome.
Did not the institute publish a Bulletin of Foreign Intelligence, advertising what was going on through the institute at Rome? If so, is that still being sent out?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We ourselves do
not'publish any bulletin of this description; it is published at the head office at Rome and distributed throughout Canada. That is the part of the service they give in return for the money they get.
I was informed that formerly 13,000 copies were sent out. Has that number been reduced?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There was a larger number previously.
Is it the policy of the department to cut down this issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We do not publish anything ourselves, as I say; it is the product of the office in Rome. We have not sent any representatives to the annual gathering these last two years, but when we do go there, if we think they are sending out too many copies, we can make representations to that effect. It has been considerably reduced.
Do I understand that the central office at Rome sends out these bulletins at the pleasure of the department and as many copies as the department wishes, and charges them to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
An allocation is
made to the sixty odd countries associated in proportion to the grant made, and the amount has been reduced of recent years to our requirement.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.	.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
I promised the leader of
the opposition (Mr. Meighen) that I would lay on the table of the House, before adjournment to-night, the correspondence which he requested last night and of which he spoke at three o'clock this afternoon. I have here a copy of all correspondence, relating to the issue of a license to the Bridge River Power Company, Limited, for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1925. This correspondence was asked for by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I came back to the House to-night ready to put on the table all the correspondence on the matter, and I have been trying to get in touch with my colleagues, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), who have further correspondence in relation to it, but unfortunately I have not been able to get in touch with them in the last few minutes. I will undertake to see that the correspondence is tabled the first thing on Monday and that we do not go on with the discussion of this matter until there has been ample opportunity for hon. gentlemen to read it.

That will be satisfactory.
